title: What AI Can and Can't Do in 2026
objective: After this level you can judge a claim about AI against what current systems reliably do and where they still fail.
summary: AI in 2026 wins olympiad gold yet reads clocks at 50.1%: a jagged frontier. NIST warns of confident falsehoods. Judge any claim by task, date and a source check.

cards.headline: Gold at the math olympiad. A coin flip on a clock.
cards.body: In 2025, AI systems reached gold-medal scores at the International Mathematical Olympiad. Yet in the 2026 AI Index, the best model read an analog clock right only 50.1% of the time. So when someone says AI can or can't do something, the honest reply is: which task, and when was it checked?

cards.headline: A jagged frontier
cards.body: Researchers call this uneven shape AI's jagged frontier. Picture a coastline rather than a wall: the edge reaches far out on some tasks, like olympiad math, and cuts deep inland on others, like telling the time from a clock face. Brilliance at one task tells you surprisingly little about the task next door. So judge a claim task by task, never by the system's best trick.

cards.headline: Fluent isn't the same as right
cards.body: There's a second catch. In 2024 NIST, the US standards agency, listed confabulation as a risk of generative AI: content stated confidently that is simply false, often called hallucination. A wrong answer arrives in the same smooth, sure voice as a right one. So the tone of an answer is no evidence at all. For anything that matters, check it against a source.

cards.headline: Date every claim
cards.body: Abilities also move fast. On one leading coding benchmark, the top AI score rose from about 60% to near 100% in a single year, the 2026 AI Index reports. So 'AI can't do X' may be out of date by next spring, and 'AI can do X' may mean X on a test, not on your problem. Ask which task, when it was measured, and whether it's the kind of task where AI is known to stumble.

cards.headline: AI claims: sized up
learned: AI's abilities are jagged: gold at math, a coin flip on clocks
NIST warns of confident but false answers (confabulation)
Scores change fast, so date every claim
Check answers that matter against a source

options.label: Top results on some hard tasks, yet failures on some easy ones
Steady progress at exactly the same rate on every task
options.rationale: Progress is uneven from task to task.

options.label: A legal border that limits where AI systems may be used
Small errors that show up only in hard math problems
options.rationale: The failures show up in easy everyday tasks, like clocks.

questions.explanation: The jagged frontier is AI's uneven ability: olympiad gold, yet a coin flip on an analog clock.

questions.prompt: A chatbot gives a confident, detailed answer about a medicine dose. What does NIST's warning about confabulation suggest?

options.label: Confident detail means it's correct
options.rationale: False content can sound just as sure.

options.label: Check the answer against a trusted source
Ask the same chatbot whether it's sure
options.rationale: Its reply would come in the same confident voice.

options.label: Trust it only if the answer is long

questions.explanation: Confabulation is confidently stated false content, so tone proves nothing: check a reliable source.

questions.prompt: An AI model is shown a photo of a clock face. From Level 5, what does it actually receive?

options.label: The time, already written out for it as text
options.rationale: It receives the picture, not the answer.

options.label: A grid of pixels, each three numbers for red, green and blue
A sound recording of the clock ticking away
The clock's own time settings, sent to it over Wi-Fi
options.rationale: A photo carries only the image.

questions.explanation: A digital photo is a grid of pixels, each three numbers from 0 to 255; the model must work out the time from those.
